---
title: "Linear models with several variables"
subtitle: "Otto & Day, chapters 7 and 9 and Primer 2, with PracticalCAS"
engine: julia
---

A linear model in several variables is a matrix: `dn/dt = A n` or
`n(t+1) = A n(t)`. Its behaviour is set by the eigenvalues of `A`. In
continuous time the origin is stable when every eigenvalue has negative real
part; in discrete time it is stable when every eigenvalue lies inside the unit
circle. For a 2×2 matrix these reduce to conditions on the trace and the
determinant.

```{julia}
using PracticalCAS
@syms a b c d λ t::nonneg
A = [a b; c d]
charpoly(A, λ)
```

```{julia}
routh_hurwitz(A)
```

```{julia}
jury(A)
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
@assert isequiv(charpoly(A, λ), λ^2 - (a + d) * λ + a * d - b * c)
rh = routh_hurwitz(A)
@assert decide(subs(rh, a => -1, b => 0, c => 0, d => -2)) === true
@assert decide(subs(rh, a => 1, b => 0, c => 0, d => -2)) === false
j = jury(A)
@assert decide(subs(j, a => 1 // 2, b => 0, c => 0, d => -1 // 3)) === true
@assert decide(subs(j, a => 2, b => 0, c => 0, d => 0)) === false
```

## Two patches with migration

Two populations grow at rates `r₁`, `r₂` and exchange migrants at rate `m`.
The population as a whole persists when the leading eigenvalue is positive.
Even if one patch is a sink (`r₂ < 0`), migration from a source keeps both
going.

```{julia}
@syms r₁ r₂ m::positive n₁ n₂
patches = ode(n₁ => r₁ * n₁ - m * n₁ + m * n₂, n₂ => r₂ * n₂ - m * n₂ + m * n₁)
J = jacobian(patches)
eigvals(J)
```

```{julia}
st = stability(patches, Dict(n₁ => 0, n₂ => 0))
st.condition
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
λs = eigvals(J)
@assert length(λs) == 2
@assert isequiv(sum(λs), r₁ + r₂ - 2m)
# a source (r₁ = 1) and a sink (r₂ = -1/2) with m = 1/10: the origin is unstable (growth)
@assert decide(subs(st.condition, r₁ => 1, r₂ => -1 // 2, m => 1 // 10)) === false
@assert decide(subs(st.condition, r₁ => -1, r₂ => -1 // 2, m => 1 // 10)) === true
```

## General solutions by diagonalisation

The solution of `dn/dt = A n` is `exp(A t) n(0)`, and that of
`n(t+1) = A n(t)` is `Aᵗ n(0)`. When `A` has distinct eigenvalues,
`A = P D P⁻¹` and both reduce to powers or exponentials of the eigenvalues.

```{julia}
M = symbolic([1 2; 2 1])
eigen(M)
```

```{julia}
matpow(M, t)
```

```{julia}
@syms x y
dsolve([x + 2y, 2x + y], [x, y], t; ic = [1, 0])
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
P = matpow(M, t)
@assert all(isequiv.(subs(P, t => 3), M^3))
sol = dsolve([x + 2y, 2x + y], [x, y], t; ic = [1, 0])
@assert isequiv(diff(sol[1], t), sol[1] + 2sol[2])
@assert isequiv(subs(sol[1], t => 0), 1)
```

## A population with juveniles and adults

Juveniles survive to adulthood with probability `s`, and adults survive with
probability `v` and produce `f` juveniles each. Here is the Leslie-type
matrix, its characteristic polynomial, and its dominant eigenvalue (the
long-term growth factor):

```{julia}
@syms f::positive s::(0, 1) v::(0, 1)
L = [0 f; s v]
charpoly(L, λ)
```

```{julia}
λs = eigvals(L)
```

The population grows (`λ > 1`) exactly when `f s + v > 1`: each adult replaces
itself through reproduction plus survival.

```{julia}
#| include: false
λ₁ = λs[2]   # the root with + sqrt
@assert isequiv(subs(λ₁, f => 2, s => 1 // 2, v => 1 // 2), (1 // 2 + sqrt(toterm(17 // 4))) / 2) ||
        isequiv(subs(λs[1], f => 2, s => 1 // 2, v => 1 // 2), (1 // 2 + sqrt(toterm(17 // 4))) / 2)
p1 = subs(charpoly(L, λ), λ => 1)            # positive iff the dominant root is below 1
@assert isequiv(p1, 1 - v - f * s)
```

```{julia}
subs(charpoly(L, λ), λ => 1)
```

With numbers, the stable stage distribution and the reproductive values come
from the right and left eigenvectors:

```{julia}
L2 = symbolic([0 4; 1//2 0])
λ₂ = sqrt(toterm(2))
stable_distribution(L2, λ₂), reproductive_values(L2, λ₂)
```

```{julia}
#| include: false
w = stable_distribution(L2, λ₂)
@assert all(isequiv.(L2 * w, λ₂ * w))
@assert isequiv(sum(w), 1)
@assert isequiv(sum(elasticity(L2, λ₂)), 1)
```
